Cairn integrates with the agents you already use, and tells you honestly what
each integration can actually do.

Still an **alpha**. Nothing here is a stability promise.

## Highlights

**Three native integrations, one lifecycle.** Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode
each connect natively. Behind them sits a single canonical seven-event
lifecycle, so no vendor event name, payload shape or ordering assumption
reaches the daemon. When a vendor changes its wire format, the adapter absorbs
it and nothing downstream moves.

**Any MCP client, without a bespoke adapter.** Clients Cairn has no specific
knowledge of integrate over the protocol itself, and the agent usage contract
is delivered through the protocol's own server-instructions mechanism.

**Capability honesty.** An integration reports two different things: what the
vendor documents, and what Cairn has actually observed on this machine. `FULL`
is earned by one ordinary session rather than declared, and it is withdrawn
when an agent updates past the evidence that earned it. `MCP_PLUS` and
`MCP_ONLY` describe the levels below it. `cairn doctor` shows which of the two
dimensions is holding a level back.

**Commands that tell you what they will do first.** `cairn agents`, `connect`,
`doctor`, `repair`, `disconnect` and `integration` each preview the changes
they would make and name what they will leave alone. Configuration edits
preserve the source: JSON/JSONC, TOML and Markdown files keep their formatting,
comments and key order outside the region Cairn owns.

**Cairn adopts an existing setup rather than competing with it.** An existing
Claude Code configuration is migrated and marked as Cairn-owned instead of
being duplicated alongside a second, conflicting entry.

**CC Switch is treated as a manager, not an agent.** Where CC Switch owns the
target application's configuration, Cairn asks it to act and never edits the
state behind it. Removals only CC Switch can perform surface as
`manager_action_required` rather than as a silent failure.

**Memory follows the project, not the agent.** A decision recorded from Claude
Code, a failure it hit, and the handoff it produced are all available to Codex
and OpenCode on the same project and task, with the producing agent recorded as
provenance. There is no per-agent memory partition and no export/import step.

**A sealed session close.** The session boundary is acknowledged as soon as
termination is durable, and the handoff is synthesized after. That is what
makes a one-second vendor handler budget survivable without giving up the
guarantee that the handoff completes.

## Supported platforms

| Platform | Status |
|---|---|
| macOS (Apple silicon, `aarch64-apple-darwin`) | Supported |
| macOS (Intel, `x86_64-apple-darwin`) | Supported |
| Linux (`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`) | Supported |
| Linux (`aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`) | Supported |
| Windows (`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`) | Supported |

The integration suites run on all three operating systems in CI, and the web
end-to-end suite now runs on hosted infrastructure rather than only locally.

## Upgrading from alpha.3

`cairn update` fetches and replaces both binaries for you. It does not restart
the daemon — it prints the two commands below, and you run them:

```bash
cairn daemon stop && cairn daemon start
```

Your local state is kept. Feature 001 and Feature 002 data written by alpha.3
remains readable, and an existing Claude Code integration is adopted rather
than replaced. To see where each agent stands after upgrading:

```bash
cairn agents
cairn doctor
```

## Install

Download the archive for your platform, verify it, and put the binaries on your
PATH. `cairn` and `cairnd` must live in the same directory — `cairn` starts the
daemon itself.

macOS and Linux:

```bash
VERSION=0.1.0-alpha.4
TARGET=aarch64-apple-darwin   # or x86_64-apple-darwin, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/Vellixia/Cairn/releases/download/v${VERSION}/cairn-v${VERSION}-${TARGET}.tar.gz
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/Vellixia/Cairn/releases/download/v${VERSION}/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS

tar -xzf cairn-v${VERSION}-${TARGET}.tar.gz
sudo install -m 0755 cairn-v${VERSION}-${TARGET}/cairn cairn-v${VERSION}-${TARGET}/cairnd /usr/local/bin/
```

Windows, in PowerShell — the archive is a `.zip`:

```powershell
$VERSION = "0.1.0-alpha.4"
$TARGET = "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"

Invoke-WebRequest "https://github.com/Vellixia/Cairn/releases/download/v$VERSION/cairn-v$VERSION-$TARGET.zip" -OutFile cairn.zip
Invoke-WebRequest "https://github.com/Vellixia/Cairn/releases/download/v$VERSION/SHA256SUMS" -OutFile SHA256SUMS

Expand-Archive cairn.zip -DestinationPath .
mkdir "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Cairn" -Force
Copy-Item "cairn-v$VERSION-$TARGET\cairn.exe","cairn-v$VERSION-$TARGET\cairnd.exe" "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Cairn"
setx PATH "$env:PATH;$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Cairn"
```

Open a new terminal so the PATH change takes effect. Then, inside a Git
repository, on any platform:

```bash
cairn init
cairn agents
cairn connect claude-code   # or codex, or opencode
```

## Container images

Only the server-side components ship as images. The local agent is native by
design.

```
ghcr.io/vellixia/cairn-server:0.1.0-alpha.4
ghcr.io/vellixia/cairn-web:0.1.0-alpha.4
```

Both are also published under an immutable `sha-<short-sha>` tag and built for
`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`. There is deliberately no `latest` tag for a
pre-release. An example stack is in
[`deploy/docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/Vellixia/Cairn/blob/main/deploy/docker-compose.yml).

## Verifying what you downloaded

- `SHA256SUMS` covers every archive, `.tar.gz` and `.zip` alike.
- `SBOM.spdx.json` describes the release contents.
- Archives and images carry GitHub build provenance attestations:

```bash
gh attestation verify cairn-v0.1.0-alpha.4-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip --repo Vellixia/Cairn
```

## Known limitations

- **Alpha.** Expect defects. Do not depend on this for anything you cannot
  reconstruct.
- **Pre-1.0 compatibility.** APIs, storage schemas and the wire protocol may
  change without a deprecation period.
- Capability levels reflect what Cairn has observed locally. A fresh install
  reports the documented level until an ordinary session provides the
  evidence, so a newly connected agent may sit below `FULL` for one session.
- On Windows the stored API token is only as private as the user-profile
  directory holding it. The `0600` mode Cairn sets on Unix has no Windows
  equivalent, and no explicit ACL is applied yet.
- Server-sync tests need a PostgreSQL service container, so that suite runs on
  Linux only.
- Sharing requires running your own Cairn server; no hosted service exists.
